name: Settled village life among Natufian foragers in the Levant
summary: Natufian hunter-gatherers in the Levant built stone houses and stayed in one place for long periods, among the first settled villages, before there was any farming.
description: From about 15,000 years ago Natufian hunter-gatherers in the southern Levant lived in long-term settlements. At Ain Mallaha (Eynan) in the Hula Basin, the Early Natufian levels hold a cluster of relatively large stone structures with walls preserved up to 1 m high, burials apparently placed below floors, and house mice that had replaced the wild mouse. Occupation was not continuous: in the Late Natufian the structures were smaller and the wild mouse returned, which is read as a shift to a more mobile life, and the degree of Natufian sedentism is still debated. A built feature at Eynan has evidence of burnt-lime plaster.

impact.note: Both sources tie this settled life to the later domestication of plants and animals and the Neolithic village economy of Southwest Asia, so many later societies descend from it (reach 2) and a line of development grew from it (generativity 2); giving up mobility for a fixed home changes the basis of a way of life (depth 3). Reach is not 3 because other foragers settled separately elsewhere.

date.label: as early as 15,000 BP (c. 13,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Dominant populations of house mice show that hunter-gatherers were living in sedentary settlements in the southern Levant as early as 15,000 BP, about 13,050 BCE.

evidence.supports: The data reveal the presence of dominant commensal populations of house mice in southern Levantine sedentary hunter-gatherer settlements as early as 15,000 B.P.

date.label: between 14,500 and 11,700 BP (c. 12,550 to 9,750 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Ain Mallaha, one of the largest known Natufian settlements, was occupied by radiocarbon dating between 14,500 and 11,700 BP, about 12,550 to 9,750 BCE.

evidence.supports: It constitutes one of the largest known Natufian settlements occupied according to C14 dating between 14,500 and 11,700 BP.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Coordinates: the White-Levy page prints '33° 08' North, 35° 57' East', which as degrees and minutes falls east of the Hula Basin and outside Israel. Read as decimal degrees (33.08, 35.57) the figures fall in the Hula Basin, where the same page puts the site, and that reading is used here; check against a gazetteer.

The Early Natufian phase at Ain Mallaha, the sedentary one, is not separately dated in these sources; the radiocarbon range covers the whole Natufian sequence at the site, and neither source says whether its BP figures are calibrated.

The paper notes that inferring mobility from Natufian material culture is debated; a source that weighs the case for year-round occupation (seasonality data, Hayonim, Wadi Hammeh 27) would strengthen the record.
Sedentism elsewhere (Jomon Japan, the Peruvian coast, the Northwest Coast) needs its own records; any of them dated earlier would overturn first_known.

research.note: Weissbrod and colleagues call these 'the first long-term hunter-gatherer settlements' and date them to 15,000 years ago, and the excavation project says Ain Mallaha is 'often described as one of the first villages'; the dataset holds no earlier settled village. The claim is the common view rather than a tested one: how permanent the occupation was is debated, and other foragers who settled (Jomon Japan, coastal Peru) are not yet recorded.

links.statement: Builders at Eynan (Ain Mallaha) used burnt-lime plaster in a bench-like built feature within the settlement.
links.scope: Architectural use of burnt-lime plaster at Eynan.
links.caveats: The laboratory study does not identify the shelter or layer for sample 86-1. Its association with the Early Natufian bench described at Shelter 1 remains unresolved.

evidence.locator: p. 224, table 1, sample 86-1, and p. 226, Eynan discussion
evidence.supports: Microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray analysis support the identification of incompletely calcined lime plaster in Eynan sample 86-1 from a bench-like built feature.

evidence.locator: The Early Natufian architectural remains, fig. 1
evidence.supports: The architectural study describes a plastered bench in Early Natufian Shelter 1 (Layer II) and discusses its debated function.
